title: Odysseus 'sacker of cities'
greek: πτολίπορθος (ptoliporthos)
short: Ptoliporthos, 'sacker of cities', recalls Odysseus' role in the fall of Troy, which this book's last song will celebrate.
body: Merry notes that in the Odyssey this epithet 'is used only of Odysseus'. In the Iliad it is given to several heroes, Akhilleus among them, but the Odyssey reserves it for the man whose stratagem of the wooden horse took Troy (cf. 1.2, 'after he had sacked the sacred citadel of Troy'). Its use at the opening of Book VIII, where Odysseus is still a nameless guest, is a quiet piece of irony, preparing for Demodocus' song of the horse (8.492-520) and for Odysseus' self-revelation, in which he identifies himself by his fame for stratagems (9.19-20). He himself uses it of himself when he taunts the Cyclops (9.504).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.3

title: Fifty-two oarsmen
greek: κούρω δὲ κρινάντων δύο καὶ πεντήκοντα (kourō de krinantōn duo kai pentēkonta)
short: Alcinous orders a new ship and fifty-two picked young men to crew it: fifty oarsmen and probably two officers.
body: Fifty is the standard crew of the Homeric pentekontor, the fifty-oared warship; the Boeotian ships in the Catalogue carry 120 men, and Philoctetes' ships fifty oarsmen each (Il. 2.509-10, 2.719-20). The extra two are perhaps a helmsman and a commander, though the Phaeacian ships, we learn, steer themselves (8.557-8). Merry notes that the dual form kourō is due to attraction to the following duo. The ship is launched 'for her first voyage' (prōtoploon), and the elaborate preparations (8.48-55) show Alcinous' haste to honour his promise, even before he knows who his guest is.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.35
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.34-6

title: Demodocus, the Phaeacian bard
greek: θεῖον ἀοιδὸν / Δημόδοκον (theion aoidon / Dēmodokon)
short: Demodocus, 'received by the people', is the court poet whose three songs in this book form a commentary on epic poetry itself.
body: Merry derives the name as populo acceptus, 'welcome to the people', from dēmos and dechesthai. The aoidos (singer) is 'divine' because his gift comes from the god or the Muse, who enables him to sing 'in whatever way his spirit prompts' (8.44-5). Demodocus sings three songs: the quarrel of Odysseus and Akhilleus (8.73-82), the love of Ares and Aphrodite (8.266-366), and the wooden horse (8.499-520). Together with Phemius in Ithaca, he is our main evidence for how Homer imagined the performance of epic poetry: a singer with a lyre (phorminx) at a feast, taking up a story 'from the point' requested by the audience (8.500). Many readers have seen in Demodocus a self-portrait of the poet.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.44
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.44

anchor: of his sight she deprived him
title: The blind singer
greek: τὸν πέρι Μοῦσ᾽ ἐφίλησε, δίδου δ᾽ ἀγαθόν τε κακόν τε· / ὀφθαλμῶν μὲν ἄμερσε, δίδου δ᾽ ἡδεῖαν ἀοιδήν (ton peri Mous' ephilēse, didou d' agathon te kakon te; / ophthalmōn men amerse, didou d' hēdeian aoidēn)
short: The Muse loved Demodocus and gave him good and evil: she took his sight but gave him sweet song. The image shaped the legend of blind Homer.
body: The paradox of the blind seer and poet, compensated for physical blindness with inner vision, is ancient and widespread; Tiresias is the prophetic counterpart. The ancient biographical tradition made Homer himself blind, a belief already present in the Homeric Hymn to Apollo, whose singer calls himself 'a blind man, who lives in rocky Chios' (172). Merry notes that the lines 'remind us of "blind Thamyris and blind Maeonides," and of our own poet', quoting Milton's lament for his blindness in Paradise Lost (3.35), where Maeonides is Homer. Pontonous' careful arrangement of the lyre on a peg and of food and wine within reach (8.65-70) gives a vivid, humane picture of a blind performer's needs.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.63-4

anchor: the quarrel of Odysseus and Achilles
title: The first song: Odysseus and Akhilleus quarrel
greek: νεῖκος Ὀδυσσῆος καὶ Πηλεΐδεω Ἀχιλῆος (neikos Odussēos kai Pēleideō Achilēos)
short: Demodocus sings of a quarrel between Odysseus and Akhilleus at a sacrificial feast, which Agamemnon welcomed because of an oracle.
body: The quarrel is not in the Iliad and is otherwise unknown. The Muse moves the singer to a song from an oimē, a 'path' or strand of song (Merry: the word 'is always used of song') whose kleos, fame, 'had then reached broad heaven'. Ancient commentators explained the quarrel as a debate after Hector's death over whether Troy would be taken by force (Akhilleus) or by craft (Odysseus); Agamemnon rejoiced because Apollo had told him at Pytho that Troy would fall when 'the best of the Achaeans' quarrelled. Gregory Nagy argued that this is a traditional theme parallel to the Iliad's quarrel between Akhilleus and Agamemnon, and that it sets two ideals of heroism, biē (might) and mētis (cunning), against each other. Some interpreters add that Agamemnon misread the oracle, which really pointed to his own quarrel with Akhilleus in Iliad 1, the true 'beginning of woe'.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.74-5
G. Nagy, The Best of the Achaeans: Concepts of the Hero in Archaic Greek Poetry (Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press, 1979)
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.73-82

title: Pytho (Delphi)
greek: Πυθοῖ ἐν ἠγαθέῃ (Puthoi en ēgatheēi)
short: Pytho is the old name of Delphi, seat of Apollo's oracle; Agamemnon crossed its 'threshold of stone' to consult the god.
body: Merry: 'Πυθώ was the oldest name of the place in Phocis where Apollo's oracle was established.' The Homeric Hymn to Apollo derives the name from the rotting (puthein) of the serpent Apollo killed there (363-74). The Iliad already knows Pytho's wealth, 'all that the stone threshold of the archer Phoebus Apollo holds within' (Il. 9.404-5), which gives the formula used here. It is the only consultation of Apollo's oracle at Pytho in Homer, and it anticipates the later prominence of Delphi in Greek life. The motif of the misunderstood oracle, so central to later tragedy and to Herodotus, may already be present: Agamemnon took a quarrel at a feast for the sign, but the real quarrel was his own with Akhilleus.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.79-81

anchor: drew it down over his head
title: Odysseus weeps behind his cloak
greek: πορφύρεον μέγα φᾶρος ... κὰκ κεφαλῆς εἴρυσσε (porphureon mega pharos ... kak kephalēs eiruse)
short: Hearing a song of his own past, Odysseus hides his face in his purple cloak and weeps, uncovering it to pour libations each time the singer pauses.
body: Covering the head is a gesture of grief and shame in Greek culture; Priam sits wrapped in his cloak in mourning (Il. 24.163). Merry explains the pharos as a large square piece of cloth worn so as to cover the left arm and shoulder. Odysseus is ashamed (aideto) to be seen weeping before the Phaeacians, but Alcinous, sitting beside him, notices (8.93-5); the scene is repeated after the third song (8.521-34). The paradox is central to the book: the songs give pleasure to the audience but pain to the man who lived them. The listener in tears before the song of his own deeds is a model of how epic poetry turns suffering into kleos, and of the different responses of participant and audience. Aeneas will weep before the pictures of Troy in Carthage (Aeneid 1.459-65).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.84

title: The Phaeacian names
greek: Ἀκρόνεώς τε καὶ Ὠκύαλος καὶ Ἐλατρεὺς / Ναυτεύς τε Πρυμνεύς τε (Akroneōs te kai Ōkualos kai Elatreus / Nauteus te Prumneus te)
short: The young Phaeacian athletes all have nautical 'speaking names': Topship, Quicksea, Oarsman, Sailor, Stern-man and so on.
body: Merry: 'Almost all Phaeacian names are taken from circumstances of seafaring life', with exceptions such as Alcinous, Arete and Laodamas. The list includes Akroneōs (top of the ship), Ōkualos (swift on the sea), Elatreus (rower), Nauteus (sailor), Prumneus (stern), Anchialos (near the sea), Eretmeus (oarsman), Ponteus (sea-man), Prōreus (bow), Thoōn (swift), Anabēsineus (embarker), and Amphialos, son of Polyneus son of Tektōn (round the sea, son of Many-ships, son of Carpenter). Such invented, transparent names are a comic touch and characterise the Phaeacians as a nation wholly devoted to the sea. They also make the catalogue entertaining to hear aloud. Euryalus, 'broad sea', will be the one who insults Odysseus.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.111-19
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.111-19

anchor: captain of sailors who are merchantmen
title: Euryalus' insult: 'you look like a trader'
greek: ἀρχὸς ναυτάων, οἵ τε πρηκτῆρες ἔασι, / φόρτου τε μνήμων (archos nautaōn, hoi te prēktēres easi, / phortou te mnēmōn)
short: Euryalus taunts Odysseus as a merchant captain mindful of cargo and profit, not an athlete: an aristocrat's sneer at trade.
body: The insult reveals the values of Homeric aristocracy, for which athletic contest is the proper activity of a nobleman and commerce, the pursuit of 'greedy gains' (kerdea harpaleōn), is base. Merry glosses prēktēres as 'traders', compares 3.72, and rejects an emendation. The charge is ironic in several ways: the Phaeacians themselves are the greatest of seafarers, and Odysseus is notorious for his interest in gain (kerdos) and his cunning. Odysseus' reply (8.166-85), a speech on how the gods distribute beauty and intelligence separately, puts Euryalus firmly in his place before he proves himself with the discus. Carol Dougherty has read the scene as part of the poem's broader engagement with trade and colonisation.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.161-4
C. Dougherty, The Raft of Odysseus: The Ethnographic Imagination of Homer's Odyssey (New York: Oxford University Press, 2001)

title: Beauty of form and beauty of speech
greek: ἀλλὰ θεὸς μορφὴν ἔπεσι στέφει (alla theos morphēn epesi stephei)
short: The gods do not give every gift to every man: one is plain but eloquent, another handsome but empty-headed, like Euryalus.
body: Odysseus' answer is a small treatise on the distribution of divine gifts and on the power of speech. The plain man whose words the god 'crowns with beauty' speaks with 'sweet modesty' (aidoi meilichiēi) and is gazed at in the city 'as a god'. Merry explains the phrase as 'puts a crown of grace upon' his words. The description fits Odysseus himself, who in the Iliad, according to Antenor, looked unimpressive until he spoke, when his words fell 'like winter snowflakes' (Il. 3.216-24). The insult to Euryalus, handsome but 'stunted in mind', exactly reverses Calypso's teasing praise of Odysseus at 5.182-3. Oratory, not just strength, is presented as a heroic gift.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.170

title: The discus throw
greek: δίσκον / μείζονα καὶ πάχετον (diskon / meizona kai pacheton)
short: Without even removing his cloak, Odysseus throws a heavier discus far beyond all the Phaeacian marks; Athena, disguised, marks the cast.
body: Merry discusses the size of the quoit and notes that the diskos was generally, as here, of stone; the humming flight and the Phaeacians ducking beneath it make a lively scene. In the funeral games of the Iliad the throwing event uses a lump of iron (solos, Il. 23.826-49). Odysseus' throw answers Euryalus' taunt in action rather than words, and Athena, 'in the likeness of a man', comments that even a blind man could find the mark, 'far the first'. Her presence, like her other disguises in Scheria, shows her steady but concealed support. The success gives Odysseus confidence to challenge all comers except his host Laodamas, whom courtesy forbids him to fight (8.204-11).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.186

title: Philoctetes the archer
greek: οἶος δή με Φιλοκτήτης ἀπεκαίνυτο τόξῳ (oios dē me Philoktētēs apekainuto toxōi)
short: Odysseus claims to be the best archer at Troy except Philoctetes, owner of Heracles' bow, without which Troy could not fall.
body: Philoctetes, abandoned on Lemnos with a festering snake-bite, is mentioned in the Iliad's Catalogue (2.718-25); later epic and tragedy (Sophocles' Philoctetes) tell how Odysseus fetched him and his bow back, since Troy could not be taken without it. In the Iliad Odysseus never uses a bow in battle, so his boast here is significant: it prepares the decisive role of the bow in the slaughter of the suitors (Books XXI-XXII). Odysseus' modest qualification, that he will not compete with the men of old, Heracles or Eurytus, leads to the story of the bow's original owner.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.219

title: Eurytus of Oechalia
greek: Εὐρύτῳ Οἰχαλιῆϊ (Eurutōi Oichaliēi)
short: Eurytus, a great archer, challenged Apollo and was killed by him; his bow, through his son Iphitus, came to Odysseus.
body: The story of Eurytus and his bow is the background of Odyssey Book XXI: Iphitus, son of Eurytus, gave the bow to the young Odysseus in Messene as a guest-gift, and Odysseus kept it at home in Ithaca, never taking it to war (21.11-41). It is with this bow that he will kill the suitors. In the Iliad Eurytus is mentioned as the king whose city Oechalia was the goal of Thamyris (Il. 2.596, 730); Merry notes that several towns bore that name, one of them in Euboea. Later tradition made Heracles sack Oechalia (as in Sophocles' Women of Trachis). The note of hubris, a mortal challenging a god, is apt in a speech which Odysseus himself presents as a warning against overreaching.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.224

anchor: changes of raiment, and warm baths
title: The Phaeacian way of life
greek: αἰεὶ δ᾽ ἡμῖν δαίς τε φίλη κίθαρίς τε χοροί τε / εἵματά τ᾽ ἐξημοιβὰ λοετρά τε θερμὰ καὶ εὐναί (aiei d' hēmin dais te philē kitharis te choroi te / heimata t' exēmoiba loetra te therma kai eunai)
short: Alcinous admits his people are no great boxers or wrestlers but love feasting, the lyre, dancing, fresh clothes, warm baths and bed.
body: Merry explains exēmoiba as clothes worn in succession, 'changes of raiment'. The frank list makes the Phaeacians the very image of a life of pleasure, and later ages read it critically. Horace calls the idle and pleasure-loving 'Alcinoi iuventus', the youth of Alcinous, who sleep till noon and care too much for their skin (Epistles 1.2.28-31). Within the poem, however, the Phaeacian pleasures of feast and song are presented with sympathy: Odysseus himself praises the banquet with song as 'the fairest thing' (9.5-11). Their pleasures also define them against the warriors of the Iliad, and against Odysseus, whose life is one of toil.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.248-9

title: Aisymnētai: the umpires
greek: αἰσυμνῆται (aisumnētai)
short: Nine officials chosen from the people level the ground and mark out the dancing floor: the aisymnētai, 'umpires' or 'stewards'.
body: Merry describes the aisymnētai as public officers who regulated the games and discusses the etymology, probably related to aisa, 'due share', as those who see to what is fitting. In historical Greece the title survived in some cities (for example at Mytilene, where Aristotle says Pittacus held the office) for magistrates, and Aristotle speaks of the aisymnētēs as an elected dictator (Politics 1285a). Here the officials prepare for the dance, which the Phaeacians perform with dazzling footwork while Demodocus plays. The orderly organisation of the games and dances, with their officials and ritual, is part of the poem's picture of a well-run community.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.258

anchor: the love of Ares and Aphrodite
title: The song of Ares and Aphrodite
greek: ἀμφ᾽ Ἄρεος φιλότητος ἐϋστεφάνου τ᾽ Ἀφροδίτης (amph' Areos philotētos eustephanou t' Aphroditēs)
short: Demodocus' second song is a comic tale of adultery among the gods: Hephaestus traps his wife Aphrodite in bed with Ares, before the laughing gods.
body: The song is the most famous and controversial passage in the Phaeacian books. Plato censured it as unfit for the young (Republic 3.390c), and ancient defenders read it as allegory: the philosopher Heraclitus (Homeric Problems 69) took the union of Ares and Aphrodite as the harmony of strife and love, and Hephaestus as fire, the craftsman. Some ancient critics suspected the lay as an interpolation. Modern scholars, following Walter Burkert, treat it as a deliberate counterpart to the main story. It is a tale of adultery discovered and punished by a cuckolded husband who wins by craft over strength, as Odysseus will over the suitors who woo his wife. The theme of marital fidelity runs through the Odyssey (Clytemnestra, Helen, Penelope), and this burlesque treats it in a comic key.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.267
W. Burkert, 'Das Lied von Ares und Aphrodite: Zum Verhältnis von Odyssee und Ilias', Rheinisches Museum 103 (1960) 130-44

title: Helius the informer
greek: Ἥλιος (Hēlios)
short: Helius, the Sun, who sees everything, tells Hephaestus of the affair; he 'kept watch' for him and brought him word.
body: The all-seeing Sun is a natural witness and informer, and Greek oaths invoke him for this reason: 'Helius, who seest all things and hearest all things' (Il. 3.277). His role here prefigures his role in the main plot. In Book XII the Sun's herald, Lampetie, tells him that Odysseus' men have eaten his cattle, and Helius demands vengeance from Zeus (12.374-90); the Odyssey's proem names this crime as the cause of the crew's destruction (1.7-9). In the song, as later, Helius' report sets punishment in motion.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.270-1

title: Lemnos and the Sintians
greek: ἐς Λῆμνον ... Σίντιας ἀγριοφώνους (es Lēmnon ... Sintias agriophōnous)
short: Hephaestus pretends to leave for Lemnos, his favourite island, home of the Sintians 'of savage speech'.
body: Lemnos, in the northern Aegean, was the chief cult centre of Hephaestus, probably because of volcanic activity once believed to occur there. In the Iliad Hephaestus tells how Zeus hurled him from heaven and he fell on Lemnos, where the Sintians cared for him (Il. 1.590-4); Merry cites this. The Sintians were a pre-Greek people, and Merry explains agriophōnos, 'of savage speech', as equivalent to 'barbarian-voiced', i.e. speaking a non-Greek language; an inscription in a non-Greek language was in fact found on Lemnos. Ares' sly mention of Hephaestus' destination as he invites Aphrodite to bed adds a mocking touch to the trick.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.283, 8.294

title: Cytherea, Aphrodite of Cythera
greek: ἐϋστεφάνου Κυθερείης (eustephanou Kuthereiēs)
short: Cytherea, 'the Cytherean', is a title of Aphrodite from the island of Cythera, south of the Peloponnese, an early centre of her cult.
body: Hesiod explains the title in his account of Aphrodite's birth from the sea-foam round the severed genitals of Ouranos: she drifted first to holy Cythera, then to Cyprus, whence she is called both Cytherea and Cyprogeneia (Theogony 188-200). Herodotus says the sanctuary at Cythera was founded by Phoenicians from the temple of Heavenly Aphrodite at Ascalon (1.105), a sign of the Near Eastern roots of her cult. Merry records a variant reading 'Aphrodite' here in some manuscripts. The epithet 'of the fair crown' (eustephanos) is also typical of her. At the end of the song she retires to her other great cult centre, Paphos on Cyprus.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.288

title: 'Unquenchable laughter' of the gods
greek: ἄσβεστος δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐνῶρτο γέλως μακάρεσσι θεοῖσι (asbestos d' ar' enōrto gelōs makaressi theoisi)
short: The gods burst into 'unquenchable laughter' at the trapped lovers, a formula first used when the gods laugh at limping Hephaestus in the Iliad.
body: The phrase occurs at Iliad 1.599, where the gods laugh to see Hephaestus bustling about as wine-pourer, ending the quarrel of Zeus and Hera. Here the joke is reversed: the laughter falls on the beautiful lovers, and the lame god has his revenge. Divine laughter in Homer expresses the gods' freedom from mortal consequences; Odysseus' own suffering throughout Book VIII contrasts with the immortals' easy mirth. The goddesses stay away 'for shame' (aidoi), while the gods crowd in the doorway, a nicely observed piece of comedy. Later 'Homeric laughter' became proverbial for uncontrollable mirth.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.326

title: 'The slow catches the swift'
greek: οὐκ ἀρετᾷ κακὰ ἔργα· κιχάνει τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν (ouk aretai kaka erga; kichanei toi bradus ōkun)
short: The gods moralise: evil deeds do not prosper; slow, lame Hephaestus has caught Ares, the swiftest god, by craft (technē).
body: Merry glosses aretai as 'prosper', comparing 19.114. The maxims summarise the song's moral, which has a wider application. Craft and intelligence overcome physical speed and strength, the principle by which Odysseus survives and wins, and the cuckolded husband takes his revenge on the handsome intruder, as Odysseus will on the suitors. The irony of 'ill deeds thrive not' is that, as Hermes and Apollo immediately show, the gods treat the affair as a joke. The lay is thus both comic relief from the sad songs of Troy and a miniature of the poem's central plot.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.329
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.329-32

title: The adulterer's fine and the bride-gifts
greek: μοιχάγρι᾽ ὀφέλλει (moichagri' ophellei)
short: Moichagria, a word found only here, is the compensation an adulterer caught in the act owed the husband; Hephaestus also demands his bride-gifts back.
body: Homeric society settled many wrongs by compensation rather than punishment: the homicide's blood-price (poinē) is shown on Akhilleus' shield (Il. 18.497-508). Moichagria (from moichos, 'adulterer', and agra, 'catch') is the corresponding payment for adultery, and Hephaestus also requires Zeus to return all the eedna, the gifts he gave for his bride (8.318-19), treating the marriage as a breached contract. The legal language gives the burlesque a solid social basis. The sequel, Poseidon's offer to stand surety for Ares, turns the comedy into a small legal drama, and the outcome (the lovers are released unpunished) makes the gods' justice the subject of the joke.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.332

anchor: the surety for a sorry knave
title: A bad man's surety
greek: δειλαί τοι δειλῶν γε καὶ ἐγγύαι ἐγγυάασθαι (deilai toi deilōn ge kai enguai enguaasthai)
short: Hephaestus refuses Poseidon's offer to guarantee Ares' payment: 'worthless are the pledges of worthless men'.
body: This is the earliest Greek reference to suretyship (enguē). The line is proverbial in style and its exact sense is disputed. Merry discusses the alternatives, among them that deilos means 'poor' ('pledges given for poor men are poor security'), that a surety given on behalf of a bad man is a bad thing to receive, or a bad thing to give. The Delphic maxim 'give a pledge, and ruin is near' (enguē, para d' atē) shows how suspicious later Greeks remained of the practice. Poseidon then binds himself to pay if Ares defaults, and Hephaestus cannot refuse so great a god (8.355-8).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.351

title: Paphos, Aphrodite's sanctuary
greek: ἐς Κύπρον ... ἐς Πάφον, ἔνθα τέ οἱ τέμενος βωμός τε θυήεις (es Kupron ... es Paphon, entha te hoi temenos bōmos te thuēeis)
short: Aphrodite withdraws to her sanctuary at Paphos in Cyprus, where the Graces bathe and anoint her and dress her in lovely clothes.
body: Paphos was Aphrodite's most famous sanctuary, with a cult of great antiquity and Near Eastern connections. Ares goes to Thrace, his home among warlike people. The scene of the Graces bathing and adorning Aphrodite recurs, in fuller form, in the Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite (58-63), which suggests a traditional type-scene of the goddess's toilette. Merry compares Virgil's Venus, who 'goes to Paphos' after meeting Aeneas, where her temple has a hundred altars steaming with incense (Aeneid 1.415-17). The ending restores divine order and beauty after the humiliation, a quiet transition back to the Phaeacian world of dance and display.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.362-3

title: Twelve kings and a thirteenth
greek: δώδεκα γὰρ κατὰ δῆμον ἀριπρεπέες βασιλῆες / ἀρχοὶ κραίνουσι, τρισκαιδέκατος δ᾽ ἐγὼ αὐτός (dōdeka gar kata dēmon ariprepees basilēes / archoi krainousi, triskaidekatos d' egō autos)
short: Alcinous is one of thirteen 'kings' (basilēes) of Scheria: the Homeric basileus is often a chief or noble rather than a monarch.
body: Alcinous is first among equals, the thirteenth, with twelve other chiefs who sit in council and contribute to gifts. Ithaca similarly has many basilēes (1.394-5), and Moses Finley used such passages to describe the Homeric basileus as the head of a powerful household whose authority rests on wealth, prestige and personal following rather than a fixed constitution. The collective gift-giving that follows, a cloak, tunic and talent of gold from each king, shows how the guest-gift system bound a community's leaders to a guest.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.390
M. I. Finley, The World of Odysseus (New York: Viking, 1954; rev. ed. 1978)

anchor: I will give him this sword
title: Euryalus' amends: the sword
greek: δώσω οἱ τόδ᾽ ἄορ παγχάλκεον (dōsō hoi tod' aor panchalkeon)
short: Euryalus makes amends with words and a bronze sword with silver hilt and ivory scabbard; Odysseus accepts with good grace.
body: Alcinous orders Euryalus to make amends 'with words and with a gift', the normal Homeric way of repairing an insult, on the model of Agamemnon's offer to Akhilleus (Il. 9.120-61). Merry notes that Homer is acquainted with ivory, but not with the elephant that produces it; the ivory is an imported luxury. The exchange of courtesies, 'Hail, Sir stranger', and Odysseus' wish that Euryalus may never miss the sword, is a model of reconciliation. Some readers detect irony: Ajax and Hector exchanged a sword and a belt in the Iliad (7.303-5), gifts which later legend made fatal to both. There is nothing ominous here; the scene confirms the Phaeacians' basic decency.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.403-4
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.401-11

title: Circe's knot
greek: δεσμὸν ... ποικίλον, ὅν ποτέ μιν δέδαε φρεσὶ πότνια Κίρκη (desmon ... poikilon, hon pote min dedae phresi potnia Kirkē)
short: Odysseus secures the chest of gifts with an intricate knot that Circe taught him: the first mention of Circe in the poem.
body: Merry: 'What she taught him was the particular complicated (poikilon) knot in which to tie the fastening.' Arete warns him to secure his treasure against theft while he sleeps on the voyage, and the knot proves useful, as nothing is stolen (13.215-18). The reference to Circe, whose story is told only in Book X, is a striking anticipation (prolepsis) and a characteristic Homeric way of suggesting a world of experiences not yet narrated. Knots and bonds connect with the song just sung (the unbreakable bonds of Hephaestus) and anticipate the bag of winds tied with silver cord, which Odysseus' companions open (10.19-27).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.448
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.447-8

title: Nausicaa's farewell: zōagria
greek: ὅτι μοι πρώτῃ ζωάγρι᾽ ὀφέλλεις (hoti moi prōtēi zōagri' ophelleis)
short: At her last appearance, Nausicaa asks Odysseus to remember her, since he owes her 'the price of his life'; he promises to pray to her as a god.
body: Merry contrasts the Iliadic sense of zōagria, a ransom paid by a captured man to the one who spares his life (cf. Il. 18.407, of Hephaestus' debt to Thetis), with its use here: 'the debt of gratitude for having saved life'. Nausicaa stands 'by the door-post of the well-built hall', the position of a woman watching from the edge of male company, and marvels at him. The exchange of only a few lines is famous for its restraint: neither mentions marriage. Odysseus answers with a vow to honour her 'as a god all my days', the highest compliment, echoing his opening comparison of her to a goddess (6.149-52). The scene closes her story with dignity and without sentimentality.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.462

title: An honour-portion for the bard
greek: νώτου ἀποπροταμὼν ... ἀργιόδοντος ὑός (nōtou apoprotamōn ... argiodontos huos)
short: Odysseus sends Demodocus a cut from the chine, the choicest portion, because singers deserve honour and reverence from all men.
body: Merry notes that the chine (nōton, back) was 'served to him as a mark of honour'. At Homeric feasts the best portion went to the most honoured guest: Agamemnon gives Ajax the whole chine after his duel with Hector (Il. 7.321-2), and Menelaus gives Telemachus a portion of it (Od. 4.65-6). Odysseus' explanation, that the Muse 'has taught them the paths (oimai) of song, and loves the tribe of minstrels', is one of Homer's statements on the dignity of the poet. Phemius in Ithaca will plead for his life on similar grounds (22.344-53). Odysseus, as guest, honours the bard on his own account, and then commissions a song.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.475
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.474-83

title: The third song: the wooden horse
greek: ἵππου κόσμον ἄεισον / δουρατέου, τὸν Ἐπειὸς ἐποίησεν σὺν Ἀθήνῃ (hippou kosmon aeison / dourateou, ton Epeios epoiēsen sun Athēnēi)
short: Odysseus asks for the song of the wooden horse, built by Epeius with Athena's help and led into Troy by Odysseus himself.
body: Odysseus requests the story of his own greatest triumph, effectively asking for his own kleos. Merry explains that Epeius built the horse with Athena's help and that Odysseus led it into the citadel 'as a thing of guile'. Demodocus' summary includes the Trojans' debate whether to break it open, throw it from the cliffs or keep it as an offering to the gods (8.505-10), the sack, and Odysseus' fight at the house of Deiphobus, Helen's new husband after Paris' death, alongside Menelaus. The horse is also described at 4.271-89 (Helen's attempt to make the hidden Greeks betray themselves) and 11.523-32. The fullest version is Virgil's in Aeneid II, where Laocoon urges its destruction and the Trojans debate as here; the Deiphobus episode is developed at Aeneid 6.494-530.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.492-3

title: Odysseus weeps like a captive widow
greek: ὡς δὲ γυνὴ κλαίῃσι φίλον πόσιν ἀμφιπεσοῦσα (hōs de gunē klaiēisi philon posin amphipesousa)
short: The conqueror of Troy weeps like a woman whose husband has fallen defending his city and who is being driven into slavery.
body: This is the most powerful 'reverse simile' in the Odyssey. Odysseus, who has just heard of his victorious sack of a city, is compared to a victim of such a sack: a wife flinging herself on her dying husband while enemy spears beat her back and shoulders and lead her into slavery. The image recalls Andromache's laments and fears for herself in the Iliad (Il. 6.450-65, 22.477-514, 24.725-45), and Briseis' grief over Patroclus (Il. 19.282-300). Critics have long discussed what the simile implies: empathy with the victims, the universal suffering of war, or the identity of victor and victim in loss. Foley's reading of reverse similes treats this one as central to the poem.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.523-31
H. P. Foley, 'Reverse Similes and Sex Roles in the Odyssey', Arethusa 11 (1978) 7-26

title: The question of the name
greek: οὐ μὲν γάρ τις πάμπαν ἀνώνυμός ἐστ᾽ ἀνθρώπων (ou men gar tis pampan anōnumos est' anthrōpōn)
short: At last Alcinous asks the stranger's name: no one is nameless, for parents name every child at birth.
body: For a day and a half Odysseus has been a nameless guest, and the poem has kept the reader aware of the delay. Alcinous' request introduces the great revelation at the start of Book IX: 'I am Odysseus, son of Laertes, known among men for all my wiles' (9.19-20). Merry's note concerns the construction of pampan. The theme of the name is crucial in what follows. Odysseus will save himself by telling the Cyclops that his name is 'Nobody' (Outis, 9.366), becoming nameless in order to survive, and will then endanger himself by boasting his real name (9.502-5). Names in this poem confer identity and fame but also vulnerability.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.552

title: The magical ships of the Phaeacians
greek: οὐ γὰρ Φαιήκεσσι κυβερνητῆρες ἔασιν (ou gar Phaiēkessi kubernētēres easin)
short: Phaeacian ships have neither pilots nor steering-oars: they understand men's minds and know every city, and cross the sea in mist without fear.
body: This is the fullest description of the Phaeacians' miraculous seafaring, foreshadowed by the simile 'swift as a thought' (7.36). The ships are intelligent agents; Merry's notes explain their 'aiming' (tituskomenai) at their destination, their ability to sense men's minds and cities, and their immunity while hidden in mist and cloud. In Book XIII one carries the sleeping Odysseus to Ithaca in a single night, moving faster than a falcon (13.81-92). The ships bridge the fabulous and the real worlds and make the Phaeacians the indispensable final helpers of the hero's nostos. Their perfection also explains Poseidon's anger: they make his sea harmless.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.557-63
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.555-63

title: Poseidon's threat to the Phaeacians
greek: μέγα δ᾽ ἧμιν ὄρος πόλει ἀμφικαλύψειν (mega d' hēmin oros polei amphikalupsein)
short: Nausithous had foretold that Poseidon, angry at their convoys, would wreck a returning Phaeacian ship and surround their city with a mountain.
body: The prophecy is fulfilled in Book XIII: after the Phaeacians take Odysseus home, Poseidon turns their returning ship to stone in sight of the harbour, and Alcinous recalls these words (13.125-87). Merry explains Poseidon's resentment of their immunity from harm, and takes the threat to mean penning the city in, so that its access to the sea is cut off. Whether the mountain actually falls is left uncertain: the Phaeacians sacrifice to Poseidon in hope of averting it, and the story leaves them at the altar (13.181-7); the reading of Zeus's advice at 13.158 was already disputed in antiquity. Alcinous' half-sceptical remark, that the god 'will bring to pass or leave unfulfilled' the prophecy as he pleases, is typical of Homeric attitudes to oracles.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.564-71
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.564-71

title: Suffering turned into song
greek: τὸν δὲ θεοὶ μὲν τεῦξαν, ἐπεκλώσαντο δ᾽ ὄλεθρον / ἀνθρώποισ᾽, ἵνα ᾖσι καὶ ἐσσομένοισιν ἀοιδή (ton de theoi men teuxan, epeklōsanto d' olethron / anthrōpois', hina ēisi kai essomenoisin aoidē)
short: Alcinous says the gods spun ruin for men at Troy so that there might be songs for future generations: suffering exists to become poetry.
body: This is one of the most striking statements about poetry in Homer. It echoes Helen in the Iliad, who says that Zeus gave her and Paris an evil fate 'so that hereafter we may be a theme of song for men to come' (Il. 6.357-8). Alcinous, speaking from the comfortable position of a listener, can see the Trojan War as material for entertainment; Odysseus, who lived it, weeps. The thought links poetry to the gods' 'spinning' of fate (cf. 7.197-8) and to kleos, the fame that only song preserves. Book VIII ends with Alcinous' questions, opening the way for Odysseus himself to become the singer of his own story in Books IX-XII.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 8.579-80
